weaknesses: The central existence claim does not match the definition. Definition 3.3 requires a bi-Lipschitz map over the full LLM function space, but Theorem 4.1 only invokes Johnson-Lindenstrauss for a finite set of K models. A genuinely low-dimensional bi-Lipschitz embedding of the entire high-dimensional function space cannot generally exist.

The practical representation is not the object analyzed theoretically. The theory uses complete logit vectors over a common output space, whereas the implementation embeds one stochastic textual generation with Qwen3-Embedding-8B. No result shows that this sentence embedding preserves logit-space or functional distances, so the implemented vectors are not proven to satisfy the proposed DNA definition.

The inheritance and genetic-determinism theorems are essentially restatements of the assumed bi-Lipschitz condition. In particular, being a fine-tuned descendant is never shown to imply small functional distance, so ancestry cannot be inferred from these results.

The main relationship evaluation is not reliable enough: only 83 positive pairs are used, randomly sampled pairs are assumed to be independent despite acknowledged missing lineage metadata, the split is apparently not model- or family-disjoint, and important details of the pair representation and SVM protocol are absent. The random and organization-based baselines are also weak.

Several alleged undocumented relationships are supported only by proximity or family resemblance, and some cross-family examples are likely false positives. Reinterpreting classifier errors as missing ground truth without independent verification makes the provenance conclusions circular.

Critical ablations and robustness tests are missing, including comparisons with unprojected response embeddings, output-text similarity and behavioral score profiles; sensitivity to embedding model, DNA dimension, prompt count, prompt formatting, decoding seed, output length, quantization, and projection seed; and retrieval of known parent models. A cross-dataset correlation of 0.7797 does not establish dataset independence.

The routing gain is small and explicitly statistically insignificant, while 11 models were removed from the referenced setup. The paper does not provide enough protocol detail or additional downstream tasks to support broad utility claims.

Neighbor-Joining produces a tree for any distance matrix, but the paper does not establish tree-additivity, validate topology against known lineage, quantify uncertainty, or provide bootstrap support. Midpoint rooting cannot establish temporal direction, and behavioral branch lengths without time normalization cannot justify claims about evolutionary speed.

The contribution beyond standard response embeddings followed by a Johnson-Lindenstrauss projection is limited, and reproducibility is weakened by the absence of released code, exact prompt samples, random matrices, software versions, detailed classifier settings, and extraction cost or runtime. weaknesses: The central existence claim is mathematically invalid under the paper's own definition. Definition 3.3 requires a bi-Lipschitz map from the entire function space F to a lower-dimensional R^L. Since the constructed F is essentially R^(N^2), such a dimension-reducing bi-Lipschitz embedding cannot exist globally. The Johnson-Lindenstrauss lemma only preserves a finite set FK; Theorem 4.1 therefore does not establish existence of the globally defined DNA claimed in the abstract and conclusion.

The inheritance and genetic-determinism theorems merely restate the two sides of the assumed bi-Lipschitz condition. The fact that one model is derived from another is unused, and the paper never proves that fine-tuning, distillation, or adaptation produces a small functional distance. Consequently, these results do not establish inheritance or determination in the substantive senses claimed.

The theory does not justify the implemented representation. The formal model outputs a vector of logits over all possible output strings, whereas the pipeline samples one stochastic textual generation and applies a nonlinear Qwen sentence encoder. No theorem or experiment supports the assertion that distances between these embeddings approximate the defined logit-space Hilbert distance. The random projection only preserves distances among the already constructed finite vectors.

There are additional formal inconsistencies: Lemma 3.2 needs strictly positive probability on every input but permits zero mass in its statement; Definition 5.1 takes an expectation of a square-rooted sum, while Lemma 5.2 analyzes the mean squared distance; and the concentration argument does not account for temperature-based stochastic decoding. Uniform boundedness of the relevant output distances is assumed but not established.

The relationship experiment is not convincing. It contains only 83 positive and 83 randomly sampled negative pairs, and splitting pairs rather than holding out models or families permits shared-model and lineage leakage. Random negatives are likely easy, the positive labels are explicitly incomplete, the SVM pair representation and tuning are unspecified, and the only baselines are random guessing and an organization heuristic. Reinterpreting false positives as discoveries using selected examples is circular.

The routing gain over EmbedLLM is only 0.007 and is acknowledged to be statistically insignificant. It is evaluated on one modified model pool after removing 11 models, without stronger routing baselines, paired significance tests, per-domain results, or analyses separating the benefit of DNA from use of the same Qwen encoder for responses and queries.

The stability conclusion is overstated. A correlation of 0.7797 between subsets of four similar English QA/reasoning benchmarks does not show independence from the sampled distribution. The number of Mantel permutations and sampled pairs is omitted, p=0.0000 is not a valid reported permutation p-value, and there are no sensitivity studies for prompts, generation seeds, decoding settings, embedding encoder, quantization, projection dimension, or projection seed.

The phylogenetic claims are unsupported. Neighbor joining assumes an approximately additive tree metric, whereas model development includes merging, distillation, and multiple ancestors and is naturally a graph. There is no quantitative comparison against known provenance, bootstrap support, held-out edge recovery, or validation of temporal ordering. Midpoint rooting cannot infer historical direction, and branch length cannot establish evolutionary speed without time calibration. Figure 6 additionally shows only a representative subset from four organizations rather than the claimed full 305-model tree.

Crucial ablations are absent, including unprojected response embeddings, alternative encoders, simple capability or output-style features, different prompt counts and domains, and existing provenance methods on compatible subsets. Thus it is unclear whether the results arise from ancestry, benchmark ability, chat templates, organization-specific response style, or the proposed construction.

Reproducibility and scalability are limited: no code or extracted DNA release is identified; exact prompts, formatting, model revisions, random seeds, projection matrix, pair features, and split-generation procedure are missing. The pipeline requires roughly 20 TB of model storage and large accelerators, yet runtime and generation cost are not reported. Overall, the practical method is a standard concatenation of response embeddings followed by random projection, and the flawed theory and weak validation do not substantiate the claimed novelty or conclusions.
